output.brief: The enrolment drop does not point to the Admissions Office. Applications and admits rose, and applicant quality held steady. Yield, meaning the share of admits who enrolled, fell from 41.8% to 34.3%. The fall is concentrated in the two tiers where merit awards were cut: Dean's went from $14,000 to $9,000 and Merit from $9,000 to $5,000. Their yield fell about 13 points each. Presidential awards and the no-award group were roughly flat. Early-action admits, who got decisions on the old timetable and were unaffected by the portal delay, lost yield as much as regular-decision admits. So the slow portal turnaround does not explain most of the loss, though it was a real service failure that hurt individual students. I can't tell whether the portal lost documents. Replacing the director would punish the wrong party and wouldn't fix the cause. Next step: take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee with a model of restoring awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, and the revenue trade-off, before award letters go out. Also set a monthly regular-decision turnaround target. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the missing-document claim is checked. I'm fairly confident about the scholarship finding; the evidence doesn't isolate the turnaround effect cleanly.
